content: A brief procedure using saline could offer lasting relief for stubborn carpal tunnel symptoms without steroids, a small clinical trial suggests. The numbness, tingling, weakness, and pain of carpal tunnel syndrome arise when the median nerve, a major nerve running from the forearm, is compressed inside a narrow passage in the wrist. Corticosteroid injections can reduce swelling and ease that pressure, but the relief may be temporary. Associated with repetitive hand and wrist movements, the condition affects roughly 5% to 10% of people over their lifetimes, and its incidence is rising. A randomized trial of 63 patients now suggests that injecting saline around the nerve under ultrasound guidance can provide relief that lasts through six months of follow-up. Adding steroids to the procedure did not significantly improve its long-term benefits. The study was published in Radiology , a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) . The procedure, called nerve hydrodissection, uses carefully injected fluid to free the nerve from surrounding adhesions, tissue attachments that can restrict its movement. Ultrasound allows clinicians to guide the injection around the affected nerve. Hydrodissection is generally combined with steroid treatment, so its effectiveness without steroids has remained uncertain. Study lead author Anindita Bose, M.D., assistant professor in the Department of Radiology at Mahatma Gandhi Medical College and Hospital in Jaipur, India, and colleagues studied patients with confirmed carpal tunnel syndrome who had not responded to conventional treatment. “Most of our patients had been suffering from carpal tunnel syndrome for months to years and did not get much relief despite trying various treatments like pain medications, splints, lifestyle modification, and corticosteroids,” said study co-author Anupama Tandon, M.D., professor in the Department of Radiodiagnosis and Imaging at University College of Medical Sciences and Guru Teg Bahadur Hospital in Delhi, India. “It came as a pleasant surprise to find that a simple procedure of dissecting the median nerve under ultrasound guidance with normal saline provided them long-term relief.” To compare the treatments, the researchers randomly divided participants into three equal groups. One received hydrodissection with normal saline, a saltwater solution. Another received hydrodissection with saline and a corticosteroid, while the third received a corticosteroid injection alone. All three treatments were guided by ultrasound. The team tracked symptoms, function, and pain using standardized clinical scores. Ultrasound measurements of the median nerve’s cross-sectional area allowed the researchers to assess changes in swelling. Follow-up assessments took place four, 12, and 24 weeks after treatment. All three groups improved significantly by four weeks, but their outcomes diverged as follow-up continued. “At 12 weeks and 6 months, both hydrodissection groups demonstrated further improvement in clinical symptoms and function, whereas patients who received corticosteroid injection alone experienced a recurrence of the symptoms, suggesting that the initial benefit was short-lived,” Dr. Tandon said. The ultrasound measurements supported the symptom and function results. The median nerve’s cross-sectional area decreased by approximately 43% to 45% after hydrodissection, compared with approximately 15% after steroid injection alone, indicating a greater reduction in nerve swelling. The lack of a significant additional long-term benefit from steroids in the hydrodissection groups matters because those drugs carry risks beyond the possibility that symptoms will return. “Traditional steroid injection for carpal tunnel syndrome often provides only temporary relief, thus requiring repeats of the procedure,” Dr. Tandon said. “Further, steroids carry risk of localized skin changes, fat thinning and tendon weakening.” Hydrodissection took an average of 15 minutes, and patients tolerated it well, with no significant immediate or delayed complications observed. Questionnaire responses indicated high satisfaction with the procedure. It was low-cost, required neither anesthesia nor hospitalization, and allowed patients to return to work within an hour. “Overall, the study suggests that ultrasound-guided saline hydrodissection is a safe, minimally invasive treatment that can provide sustained clinical and morphological improvement in patients with refractory carpal tunnel syndrome,” Dr. Tandon said. “Thus, hydrodissection merits to be a minimally invasive option for mild to moderate carpal tunnel syndrome and can defer and even alleviate the need for surgery.” The researchers said larger studies across multiple centers, with longer follow-up, are needed. They have already launched a study comparing the long-term effectiveness of different fluids used for hydrodissection in carpal tunnel syndrome, including dextrose versus saline. “This trial features an extended follow-up period to track long-term patient outcomes and establish the true durability of the treatment,” Dr. Tandon said. Reference: “Efficacy of US-guided Hydrodissection for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: A Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial” by Anindita Bose, Anupama Tandon, Gopesh Mehrotra, Siddharth Maheshwari and Ayush Khandelwal, 6 October 2026, Radiology . Seven molecules in human milk could help explain how a mother’s nutrition connects with her baby’s growth, offering a window into the biology of milk production. Human milk contains thousands of nutrients, metabolites, proteins, immune factors, and other molecules, yet researchers have often studied those components one at a time. Much remains unknown about how the gland that produces milk shapes this mixture and how differences in its composition relate to infant growth. By examining those molecules together, a team led by researchers at NYU Grossman School of Medicine identified seven candidate biomarkers associated with maternal nutritional status, infant growth, and biological processes within the mammary gland. Their study, published in Science , analyzed 1,543 milk samples from three geographically and nutritionally diverse cohorts in Canada, Pakistan, and Burkina Faso. The mammary gland prepares for milk production during pregnancy, undergoing hormonal changes that guide cell specialization, tissue and immune remodeling, and metabolic programming. Lactation becomes the main expression of that preparation after delivery. Like the placenta during pregnancy, the gland then serves as an interface between mother and child, connecting maternal biology and nutrition with the developing infant. “Human milk gives us a rare, non-invasive window into the biology of the lactating mammary gland,” said Liat Shenhav, PhD, the study’s senior author and an assistant professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, with appointments in the Institute for Systems Genetics, the Department of Microbiology, and the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology. “By looking at molecular patterns across diverse populations, we can begin to identify shared features of mammary function and understand how maternal nutritional and metabolic state relates to milk composition and infant growth.” The study is one of two complementary papers published in Science from the International Milk Composition (IMiC) Consortium. Conducted in collaboration with Meghan Azad of the University of Manitoba and funded by the Gates Foundation, this international research effort brought together more than 1,000 mother-infant pairs and profiled more than 25,000 molecular features in human milk. For the NYU-led analysis, researchers integrated measurements of metabolites, proteins, micronutrients such as vitamins, macronutrients such as carbohydrates, and human milk oligosaccharides, a group of complex sugars. This approach, called multi-omics, examines several types of molecules together to build a fuller picture of a biological system. The team analyzed these measurements alongside infant growth data using computational tools, including machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence. In two randomized nutritional trials, maternal supplementation promoted recovery or stability in growth among infants at higher risk of poor growth. The molecular analyses also revealed a shared pattern in milk composition associated with both supplementation and infant growth. The companion study examined which milk components could be changed through maternal nutrition. It found that supplementation during lactation increased several B vitamins in milk, while many other components remained comparatively stable. “The studies show that human milk is neither fixed nor simply a reflection of what a mother eats,” said Shenhav. “Some components respond to maternal nutrition, while others remain stable or appear to reflect broader biological states within the mammary gland. Understanding that distinction is essential if we want to design interventions that meaningfully support maternal and infant health.” Mammary cells make and release milk components, while an epithelial barrier regulates what passes between the bloodstream and milk. Tissue remodeling reshapes the milk-producing tissue, and immune and repair processes protect the gland and help it recover from stress or injury. The researchers mapped milk’s molecular patterns onto these interconnected functions. Seven molecules contributed most consistently to the patterns associated with maternal nutritional status and infant growth. Four were short-chain acylcarnitines, called C2, C3, C4, and C5, which help cells process nutrients for energy. The remaining three were the amino acid lysine, the complex sugar 6′ sialyllactose, a human milk oligosaccharide, and the mineral selenium. Together, these candidate biomarkers captured complementary aspects of mammary function, extending beyond established measures of blood-milk barrier permeability, or how readily substances cross that barrier. The acylcarnitines showed the strongest links across the gland’s different functions, particularly C5. Higher C5 levels were associated with molecular signatures of reduced milk synthesis and with patterns related to tissue remodeling and immune activity. C5’s prominence prompted the researchers to examine how maternal nutrition might influence acylcarnitine levels. Acylcarnitine metabolism depends on coenzyme A, or CoA, a molecule central to energy and fat metabolism. The body makes CoA from pantothenic acid, better known as vitamin B5. Drawing on this established biology and associations across the cohorts, the researchers proposed that too little available vitamin B5 may restrict CoA-dependent metabolism and alter acylcarnitine profiles, potentially allowing C5 to accumulate. “Our findings demonstrate the intimate link between maternal nutrition, metabolic health and mammary function, highlighting the importance of an integrative approach to supporting maternal and infant health,” said first author Dr. April Jauhal of the Shenhav lab at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. “One plausible route linking maternal nutrition to mammary metabolism in our data is via the pantothenic-CoA-C5 metabolic pathway, and we are currently investigating the functional role of this pathway in mammary biology and lactation.” The Shenhav Lab is developing a framework that combines computational and experimental work to test potential nutritional bottlenecks that may constrain mammary metabolism and milk production. These include the proposed pathway involving vitamin B5, coenzyme A, and C5. “Ultimately, we want to understand milk in the context of the biology that produces it,” said Shenhav. “The mammary gland sits at a critical interface between maternal physiology and the developing infant. By understanding how maternal metabolism influences mammary function and milk composition, we can begin to uncover the biological pathways linking maternal nutritional status with infant growth.” Milk can be collected repeatedly without invasive procedures, allowing researchers to follow mammary biology over time. The lab is also studying colostrum, the earliest milk, and transitional milk, which precedes mature milk. Researchers want to understand how mammary functional states emerge during the transition from pregnancy to mature lactation, and whether early molecular changes in milk reflect the development of the gland’s metabolic, barrier, and secretory functions. Reference: “Shared patterns of human milk composition link mammary gland function to infant growth” by April Jauhal, Bianca Cordazzo-Vargas, Daniel Sunko, Pratima Niroula, Lishi Deng, Laeticia Celine Toe, Ameer Muhammad, Aneela Pasha, Yasir Shafiq, Naveed Iqbal, Waqasuddin Khan, Andrew Mertens, Kelsey Fehr, Joann M. A small trial in older adults uncovered subtle gut changes and hints of mood improvement with daily blueberry powder, but no clear benefit over placebo. Inside the gut, the fiber and dark pigments in blueberries encounter a crowded community of microbes. Those ingredients could change the microbes and the substances they produce, raising the possibility that eating the fruit might influence mood. Establishing whether those microscopic changes actually ease depressive symptoms requires evidence that reaches beyond the gut. Courtney L. Millar, PhD, and her colleagues explored that possibility in a three-month pilot study of sedentary adults 65 and older with mild depressive symptoms. Participants who consumed blueberry powder daily showed a greater, more consistent reduction in symptoms than those given a placebo. The difference between the groups was not statistically significant, however, leaving the apparent benefit uncertain. “Fiber and anthocyanins in blueberries have potential to modify the gut microbiome and metabolites that are relevant to depression in older adults,” said Millar, the study’s lead author and an assistant scientist II at Hebrew SeniorLife’s Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research. Anthocyanins are the pigments that give blueberries their rich color, while metabolites are substances produced through chemical processes, including those carried out by microbes. Participants were randomly assigned to consume either 48 grams, about 1.7 ounces, of blueberry powder each day or a matched placebo powder. The blueberry portion represented approximately two cups of fresh berries. The trial was double-blind, meaning neither the participants nor the researchers assessing them knew who was receiving which powder. Millar’s team paired questionnaires measuring depressive symptoms with laboratory analyses of stool samples collected before and after the intervention. “Our objective was to preliminarily determine the effect of blueberry consumption on the gut microbiome, metabolites, and depressive symptoms,” said Millar, who is also an assistant professor of medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School. Reading microbial DNA allowed the researchers to measure which species and genes were present and how abundant they were. Separate chemical analyses measured short-chain fatty acids, substances produced by gut microbes. Together, these measurements let the team examine both the microbial community and some of its chemical products. Several categories of genes associated with microbial enzymes changed significantly within the blueberry group. One involved polyamine-transporting ATPase, which the researchers describe as participating in the production of the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid, or GABA. Changes in the abundance of those genes do not, by themselves, demonstrate that the microbes produced more GABA or that it affected participants’ mood. Other measurements remained unchanged, including the abundance of microbial species, the metabolic pathways assessed, and the short-chain fatty acids measured in stool. The genetic findings therefore represented a narrow change within the gut microbiome, without a corresponding change in those measured chemical products. Eighteen older adults completed the study, including 10 who consumed blueberry powder daily and eight who received a placebo. Researchers observed subtle shifts in microbial genes in the blueberry group, alongside greater reductions in depressive symptoms, pointing to a possible connection between blueberry compounds, the gut microbiome, and mood. Reference: “A pilot study of daily blueberry intake modulates the gut microbiota enzyme commissions in older, sedentary adults with mild depressive symptoms” by Courtney L. Millar, Mohit P. Chopra, Xochitl Morgan, Emily A. Green, Alex Wolfe, Kerry A. Pierce, Lidan Gao, Christopher N. Blesso, Alyssa B. Dufour, Douglas P. Kiel and Lewis A.
